pos: v. (to go or come into a place, state, or covenant; rendering Hebrew bo, Greek eiserchomai)
etymology: From French entrer, Latin intro, within. Scripture makes the word a doorway word: there is an inside and an outside, a gate that is strait and a gate that is wide, and the whole gospel turns on which one a man goes through.
biblical_def: To enter is to cross from outside to inside, and Scripture never treats that crossing as automatic. Our Lord sets two gates before every hearer and commands the harder one: “Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able” (Luke 13:24). The verse is fatal to every easy assumption about entrance. Many seek and are not able, which means the door is not opened by desire, sincerity, or effort, but by Christ who is Himself the door. Entrance therefore has a manner as well as a fact. The Psalmist prescribes it: “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name” (Psalm 100:4). A man does not stroll into the presence of God; he comes through appointed gates in an appointed spirit. The word also carries the believer's end, for the reward at the last is stated as an entering: “enter thou into the joy of thy lord” (Matthew 25:21). Between the strait gate and that final welcome lies a labour the Apostle does not soften — “Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief” (Hebrews 4:11). Rest is entered by labouring, and unbelief is what keeps a generation standing outside.
webster_summary: To go or come into a place; to pass within the boundary of anything; to engage in, to become a member of, to set down in writing. Scripture uses the word chiefly of entering God's gates, His rest, and His joy — each by an appointed way and never by presumption.
webster_full: ENTER, v.t. [Fr. entrer; L. intro, within.] To move or pass into a place, in any manner whatever; to come or go in; to walk or ride in; to flow in; to pierce or penetrate.
2. To advance into, in the progress of life; as, to enter on the twentieth year of age.
3. To begin in a business, employment or service; to engage in.
4. To become a member of; as, to enter a society; to enter the church.
5. To set down in writing; to set down in a book or register; as, to enter a name; to enter a memorandum.
ENTER, v.i. To go or come in; to pass into; as, to enter into a house. To engage in; as, to enter into business. To be initiated in.
scriptures: Luke 13:24
Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.
Psalm 100:4
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
Matthew 25:21
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Hebrews 4:11
Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.
corruption_summary: Entrance has been made automatic. Where Scripture sets a strait gate that many seek and cannot pass, the modern assumption is that everyone is already inside and the gate is a formality — which empties both the warning and the welcome.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning error is not that men deny heaven but that they assume entrance into it. Sermons that once pressed our Lord's own command to strive now describe a God whose door has no frame, and the funeral of any man whatever is preached as an accomplished entering. Scripture will not carry it. The Lord Jesus says plainly that many will seek to enter in and shall not be able, and He says it in answer to a direct question about how many are saved. To make entrance universal is to make His answer meaningless and His gate ornamental.

The opposite corruption travels in devotional dress: the notion that entering God's presence is a technique — the right music, the right atmosphere, the right emotional pitch — rather than a way opened by blood. Psalm 100 does prescribe a manner, thanksgiving and praise, but the manner rests on an accomplished work, not on the worshipper's intensity. Recover the plain shape of the word: Christ is the door (John 10:9); entrance is by Him, in thanksgiving, unto rest, and the labour Hebrews commands is the labour of faith against unbelief, not the labour of working a passage.
roots_summary: Hebrew bo (to come in, go in, enter) is the ordinary verb of coming into land, house, or covenant; Greek eiserchomai (to go into) is the Gospels' word for entering the kingdom, the strait gate, and the joy of the Lord.
roots_lines: Hebrew bo (H935) — to come in, go in, enter; used of entering the ark, the land, and the sanctuary, and so of every appointed crossing.
Hebrew sha'ar (H8179) — gate; the fixed place of entrance, of judgment, and of the elders' counsel, which is why entering “his gates” is covenantal language (Psalm 100:4).
Greek eiserchomai (G1525) — to enter, go in; the verb of Luke 13:24 and of entering into the kingdom of God.
Greek eisodos (G1529) — an entrance, a coming in; used of the entering in that the gospel had among the Thessalonians.
Greek thura (G2374) — a door; our Lord's self-designation, which fixes entrance to His Person rather than to a method.
usage: “Strive to enter in at the strait gate” — entrance is commanded and contested, not assumed.
“Enter into his gates with thanksgiving” — the manner of coming is prescribed with the fact of coming.
“Enter thou into the joy of thy lord” — the last word of the gospel is an invitation inward.

pos: v. (to change direction; to forsake one course for another; rendering Hebrew shuwb, Greek epistrepho)
etymology: From Saxon tyrnan, Latin torno, to round or shape on a lathe. In Scripture the word is almost never geometric and almost always moral: a man is going one way, and God commands him to face the other.
biblical_def: Turn is the Old Testament's great word for repentance, and it is a word about direction rather than feeling. The LORD doubles it for urgency and grounds it in His own disposition: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11). Two things are fixed there at once. God takes no delight in the destruction of sinners, and the sinner's turning is nevertheless commanded rather than optional. The prophets press the same verb inward so that no one may turn with the feet only: “turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). Turning is to a Person before it is from a practice, and the heart is named as the organ that must move. The covenant promise attaches to it: when a people humble themselves, pray, seek His face, “and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). Wisdom issues the same summons with a promise of the Spirit — “Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you” (Proverbs 1:23) — which is why turning is a grace given, not a work achieved.
webster_summary: To move round; to change position or direction; to alter in course, form, or disposition; to convert. Scripture's dominant use is moral: to turn from evil ways unto the LORD, which is repentance under its plainest name.
webster_full: TURN, v.t. [Sax. tyrnan; L. torno, to round or shape in a lathe.] To cause to move in a circular course; to cause to revolve; as, to turn a wheel.
2. To change or alter in position; to shift; as, to turn the face to the east.
3. To alter in course or direction; to divert; as, to turn the current of a stream.
4. To change; to transform; to convert; as, to turn water into ice; and figuratively, to turn the heart.
5. To reverse; to put the inside outward, or the lower part upward.
TURN, v.i. To move round; to have a circular motion. To change sides, opinion, or conduct; to be converted; as, to turn from the error of one's way.
scriptures: Ezekiel 33:11

Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?
Joel 2:12
Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:
2 Chronicles 7:14

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
Proverbs 1:23
Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you.
corruption_summary: Turning has been reduced to self-improvement — a change of habits, a new leaf, a better version of the same man — where Scripture means forsaking a way and facing a Person, with the heart moved first.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest modern flattening treats turning as resolution. A man alters his routine, drops a vice, adopts a discipline, and calls it repentance. But Ezekiel's doubled imperative is addressed to men under sentence of death and offers life, not improvement; and Joel demands the heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning, precisely because the outward alteration can be performed by an unturned heart. Where the word is preached as behaviour modification, the hearer is left doing what an unregenerate man can do, and the promise attached to the real thing never reaches him.

A second corruption cuts the other way, treating turning as a change of mind only, so that a man may hold his sin and adjust his opinion of it. Scripture joins the two without apology: the wicked turns from his way, and the covenant promise of 2 Chronicles 7:14 is suspended on turning from wicked ways, not on revising an estimate of them. Recover the biblical order — the Spirit poured out at Wisdom's reproof (Proverbs 1:23) turns the heart, the heart turns the man, and the man forsakes the way. Turning is God's gift before it is the sinner's duty, and it is genuinely the sinner's duty.
roots_summary: Hebrew shuwb (to turn back, return, restore) is the prophets' standard call to repentance; Greek epistrepho (to turn about, turn toward) carries it into the New Testament as conversion.
roots_lines: Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, return; the great prophetic verb of repentance, used over a thousand times and doubled for urgency in Ezekiel 33:11.
Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to be sorry, to repent; the affectional side of turning, distinguished from shuwb's directional force.
Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to turn toward; used of Gentiles turning to God from idols.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; the mind's change that epistrepho shows in the feet.
Hebrew panah (H6437) — to turn the face; the bodily posture behind the moral figure, since a man faces what he serves.
usage: “Turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways” — the doubled command marks urgency, not repetition for its own sake.
“Turn ye even to me with all your heart” — the turning is toward a Person and begins inwardly.
“Turn from their wicked ways” — the covenant promise of healing is attached to a forsaken way.

pos: v. (to come back to a place, state, or person; rendering Hebrew shuwb, Greek hupostrepho)
etymology: From French retourner, to turn again. Scripture bends the word two ways at once: man returns to the dust by the curse, and man returns to the LORD by mercy — and the second is the only escape from the first.
biblical_def: Return is turn with a homeward direction: the going back to a place one came from, or a Person one has left. The curse gave the word its first and heaviest sense: “till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Genesis 3:19). Every man is already on a return journey, and left to himself it ends in the dust he was taken from. Against that the prophets set the other return, and they set it with a promise of abundance: “Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” (Isaiah 55:7). Two things must go before the returning — a forsaken way and forsaken thoughts — and two things follow it, mercy and abundant pardon. The LORD calls even the unfaithful back by name: “Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD; and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you: for I am merciful” (Jeremiah 3:12). The soul's own returning is addressed to itself in the Psalms: “Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee” (Psalm 116:7), where rest is a place the soul has wandered from and may come home to.
webster_summary: To come or go back to the same place or state; to revert; to repay or render back. In Scripture the word carries both the curse's return to dust and the sinner's return to the LORD, who abundantly pardons.
webster_full: RETURN, v.i. [Fr. retourner; re and tourner, to turn.] To come or go back to the same place from which one departed; as, to return from a journey.
2. To come back to the same state or condition; as, to return to a former practice.
3. To answer; to reply; to make a reply or report.
RETURN, v.t. To bring, carry or send back; as, to return a borrowed book.
2. To repay; to give in requital or recompense; as, to return good for evil.
3. To render back or transmit officially; as, to return a writ; to return an account.
scriptures: Genesis 3:19
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Isaiah 55:7
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
Jeremiah 3:12

Go and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD; and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you: for I am merciful, saith the LORD, and I will not keep anger for ever.
Psalm 116:7
Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee.
corruption_summary: Return has been sentimentalized into homecoming without repentance — a warm reunion that skips the forsaken way and the forsaken thoughts Isaiah puts before it.
corruption_paragraphs: Much modern preaching on returning to God keeps the affection and drops the terms. The prodigal is invoked, the Father's run and kiss are dwelt upon, and the son's own confession is passed over. Isaiah 55:7 does not permit it: the wicked forsakes his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and then returns. Mercy and abundant pardon are promised on the far side of that forsaking, not instead of it. Where the terms are dropped, hearers are taught to expect the welcome without the turning, and the doctrine of repentance quietly disappears while its warmest illustration is retold.

There is a second and colder error that treats Genesis 3:19 as the whole story — man returns to dust, and nothing further is to be said. That is the creed of the age in its plainest form, and it is why the modern funeral so often has nothing to say. Scripture holds both returns together and subordinates the first to the second: the body goes to the ground under the curse, and the soul is called home to its rest because “the LORD hath dealt bountifully” (Psalm 116:7). Recover the pairing, and the word regains its weight in both directions.
roots_summary: Hebrew shuwb (to turn back, return) serves both the curse's return to dust and the covenant call to return to the LORD; Greek hupostrepho (to turn back) and anastrepho (to turn again) carry the ordinary sense in the New Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, return, restore; the single verb behind Isaiah's call and Jeremiah's summons to backsliding Israel.
Hebrew meshuwbah (H4878) — backsliding, turning away; the noun formed from shuwb, naming the condition the return reverses.
Hebrew 'adamah (H127) — ground, earth; the destination of the curse's return in Genesis 3:19.
Greek hupostrepho (G5290) — to turn back, to return; the narrative verb of the Gospels and Acts.
Greek epistrophe (G1995) — a turning about, conversion; the noun naming the return as an accomplished thing.
usage: “Unto dust shalt thou return” — the curse states a return no man escapes by his own strength.
“Let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him” — the terms precede the promise.
“Return unto thy rest, O my soul” — the believer preaches the word to his own soul.

pos: v. (to go by, move on, or come to an end; rendering Hebrew 'abar, Greek parerchomai)
etymology: From French passer, Latin passus, a step. Scripture uses the word for two opposite movements — the world passing away under judgment, and the LORD passing over His people in mercy.
biblical_def: To pass is to move by and be gone, and Scripture applies it first to the world men treat as permanent: “the fashion of this world passeth away” (1 Corinthians 7:31). The Apostle's word is not substance but fashion — the shape, the arrangement, the going order of things — and it is already in motion. Our Lord fixes the contrast that gives the doctrine its comfort: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). The most solid things a man can name are the passing ones, and the least visible thing, the word of Christ, is what stands. The same verb turns to mercy at the Passover, where the LORD passes by the houses marked with blood: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you” (Exodus 12:13). Judgment moves through the land and steps over a house, and the reason given is not the character of those inside but the blood outside. The word finally describes what conversion does to a man's past: “if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). What passes there is not memory but dominion.
webster_summary: To move from one place to another; to go by; to elapse; to be transferred; to come to an end. Scripture's two great uses are the world's passing away under judgment and the LORD's passing over His people in mercy.
webster_full: PASS, v.i. [Fr. passer; L. passus, a step.] To move, in almost any manner; to go; to proceed from one place to another.
2. To go by; to move by or beyond; as, the procession passed.
3. To elapse; to be spent; as, the time passes rapidly.
4. To go away; to depart; to vanish; to cease; as, the storm has passed.
5. To be transferred from one owner to another; as, an estate passes by deed.
PASS, v.t. To go by, beyond, over or through; to omit; to overlook; to transcend; as, to pass a house; to pass the bounds of reason.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 7:31
And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
Matthew 24:35
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
Exodus 12:13

And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt. to
2 Corinthians 5:17
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
corruption_summary: The passing of this world is treated as a poetic sentiment rather than a coming fact, and “passing away” has become a euphemism that lets men speak of death without naming it or its judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern speech has taken the Bible's solemn verb and made it a softener. A man no longer dies; he passes. The substitution looks like kindness and functions as evasion, because the word that Scripture uses to announce the end of the world is put to work hiding the end of a life. Where death cannot be named, judgment cannot be named either, and the comfort that Scripture actually offers — that the words of Christ do not pass away when heaven and earth do — is never reached. Plain speech about death is the doorway to real consolation, and euphemism bars it.

The deeper corruption is practical rather than verbal: living as though the fashion of this world were the durable thing. The Apostle wrote 1 Corinthians 7:31 to men buying, marrying, and using the world, and he did not forbid these things; he relativized them by a fact. What passes is to be used and not leaned upon. Recover the ordering — heaven and earth pass, His word does not; the plague passes over the blood-marked house; old things are passed away in Christ — and the word stops being a euphemism and becomes a discipline.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'abar (to pass over, through, or by) is the verb of crossing Jordan and of the Passover itself; Greek parerchomai (to pass by, pass away) carries the eschatological sense in our Lord's words.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abar (H5674) — to pass over, through, or by; used of crossing rivers, of transgressing a command, and of the LORD passing before Moses.
Hebrew pacach (H6452) — to pass over, to spare; the verb behind pesach, the Passover, in Exodus 12:13.
Greek parerchomai (G3928) — to pass by, to pass away; the word of Matthew 24:35 for heaven and earth.
Greek paragō (G3855) — to lead past, to pass away; used of the world and its fashion going by.
Greek schēma (G4976) — fashion, outward form; the precise thing Paul says is passing in 1 Corinthians 7:31.
usage: “The fashion of this world passeth away” — the arrangement of things is temporary, not the creation itself.
“My words shall not pass away” — the permanence men assign to heaven and earth belongs to Christ's speech.
“I will pass over you” — judgment steps over a house on account of blood.

pos: v. (to bear or convey from one place to another; rendering Hebrew nasa, Greek bastazo)
etymology: From Norman French carier, to convey in a vehicle. In Scripture the word most often has God for its subject: it is He who carries, and the burden He carries is His people.
biblical_def: Carry means to bear a weight from one place to another, and the Bible's striking use of it puts the LORD in the position of the bearer. He binds Himself to it for the whole length of a life: “And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you” (Isaiah 46:4). The argument runs from creation to preservation — the One who made is the One who will bear — and it is aimed at men in their weakest season, when strength is spent and the hair is grey. The shepherd figure gives the same truth its tenderest form: “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). Carrying is discriminating; the lambs and the burdened are singled out for it. Israel's whole history is summed up in the verb: “he bare them, and carried them all the days of old” (Isaiah 63:9), and the same verse says that in all their affliction He was afflicted. Over against what God carries, the Apostle sets what man cannot: “we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out” (1 Timothy 6:7).
webster_summary: To bear, convey, or transport from one place to another; to sustain; to effect or accomplish. Scripture's dominant use makes God the carrier of His people from the womb to hoar hairs, and man the carrier of nothing out of this world.
webster_full: CARRY, v.t. [Norm. carier, from car, a vehicle.] To bear, convey or transport, by sustaining and moving the thing carried, either by bodily strength, upon a beast, or in a vehicle.
2. To convey; to transport; as, a ship carries a cargo.
3. To effect; to accomplish; to prevail; to gain the object; as, to carry a point or measure.
4. To bear out; to face through; as, to carry a matter with a high hand.
5. To support or sustain; as, a pillar carries the weight of the arch.
CARRY, v.i. To convey; to propel; as, a gun carries well, that is, throws its ball to a great distance.
scriptures: Isaiah 46:4
And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.
Isaiah 40:11
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.
Isaiah 63:9
In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them: in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; and he bare them, and carried them all the days of old.
1 Timothy 6:7
For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
corruption_summary: The therapeutic register has made carrying a private psychological freight — what a man “carries” within — displacing the Bible's use, in which God carries His people and man carries nothing out of the world.
corruption_paragraphs: Current speech is full of what people carry: burdens described as interior conditions to be processed, managed, and eventually set down by technique. The vocabulary is not neutral. It relocates the weight from a Bearer to a self, and it renames sin and affliction as conditions rather than as things suffered under God's hand and borne away by Christ. Scripture's grammar is the reverse. The subject of the verb is God — “I will carry, and will deliver you” — and the sufferer's comfort is not that he has learned to bear well but that Another bears him. Affliction remains real; Isaiah 63:9 says the LORD was afflicted in His people's affliction, which no technique can match. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic use of 'carry' in order to rebut it

The second and older corruption is acquisitive: living as though a man could carry something out. Paul's flat statement in 1 Timothy 6:7 is set immediately before his warning about the love of money, and it functions as the argument for contentment. Nothing came in with us and nothing goes out with us; therefore godliness with contentment is the great gain. Recover both halves of the word — God carries His people, His people carry out nothing — and both anxiety and covetousness lose their footing at once.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasa (to lift, bear, carry) is the verb of bearing burdens, bearing sin, and lifting up the countenance; Greek bastazo (to bear, carry) and phero (to bring, bear) carry the sense into the New Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift, carry, bear; used of bearing burdens, bearing iniquity, and of God bearing His people.
Hebrew 'amac (H6006) — to load, to lade; the verb behind the LORD who daily loadeth us with benefits.
Hebrew cheyq (H2436) — bosom; the place the lambs are carried in Isaiah 40:11.
Greek bastazo (G941) — to take up, bear, carry; used of bearing one another's burdens.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, bring, carry; used of Christ upholding all things by the word of His power.
usage: “Even to hoar hairs will I carry you” — the promise is aimed at the end of strength, not its prime.
“Carry them in his bosom” — the shepherd's carrying singles out the weakest of the flock.
“We can carry nothing out” — the ground of contentment is stated as plain fact.

pos: v. (to take away, put out of a place, or displace; rendering Hebrew cuwr, Greek metabaino)
etymology: From Latin removere, to move back or away. Scripture uses the word for the greatest mercy and the gravest threat: God removes transgressions, and God removes candlesticks.
biblical_def: To remove is to take a thing out of its place, and Scripture measures the mercy of it by distance: “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12). The figure is chosen with care. North and south have poles and a fixed span between them; east and west have none, and the distance cannot be closed. That is the measure of the removal of a believer's sin, and it is God who does the removing. The same verb turns to warning when what is removed is a privilege: “I will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent” (Revelation 2:5). A church may keep its address and lose its light, and the Lord names the condition on which the lampstand stays. There is also a removal men are forbidden to attempt: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Proverbs 22:28). The landmark was the boundary stone of an inheritance, and shifting it stole land while appearing to touch nothing. Finally the word measures faith's object rather than its size: “If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove” (Matthew 17:20).
webster_summary: To move from one place to another; to take away; to displace; to banish or destroy. Scripture uses it of God removing transgressions to an unmeasurable distance, of removing a church's candlestick, and of the landmark no man may remove.
webster_full: REMOVE, v.t. [L. removeo; re and moveo, to move.] To cause to change place; to put from its place in any manner; to take or carry away.
2. To displace from an office; as, to remove an officer from his station.
3. To take away; to cause to leave a person or thing; to banish or destroy; as, to remove a disease.
4. To dispossess; to eject from possession.
REMOVE, v.i. To change place in any manner; to move from one place or residence to another; as, to remove from London to Paris.
REMOVE, n. Change of place; departure; the act of removing; also, a step or degree in any scale of gradation.
scriptures: Psalm 103:12
As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
Revelation 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Proverbs 22:28
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Matthew 17:20

And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.
corruption_summary: The ancient landmark is precisely what the age is committed to removing — inherited boundaries of sex, marriage, office, and worship are treated as arbitrary stones rather than as fathers' settlements under God.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 22:28 forbids a quiet theft. Moving a boundary stone by a few feet took a neighbour's inheritance without the appearance of robbery, and the law repeats the prohibition (Deuteronomy 19:14) because the crime is hard to see and hard to reverse. The principle governs more than fields. Where the created boundary of male and female is treated as a stone that may be shifted, where marriage's bounds are moved, where the offices Christ set in His church are redrawn, the same quiet theft occurs: an inheritance received from the fathers is taken from children who never consented and cannot easily recover it.

The second corruption is the assumption that removal runs only one direction, that a church once lit is lit permanently. Revelation 2:5 says otherwise to a congregation that had orthodoxy, labour, and patience, and had left its first love. The candlestick is removable, and repentance is the stated condition of its remaining. Set beside Psalm 103:12 the two removals define the Christian's hope and fear rightly: what God removes from the believer is his transgression, immeasurably; what God may remove from an unrepentant church is its light.
roots_summary: Hebrew cuwr (to turn aside, remove) and racaq (to be far, to remove far) give Psalm 103:12 its distance; Greek metabaino (to pass over, remove) and kineo (to move) carry the New Testament senses.
roots_lines: Hebrew cuwr (H5493) — to turn aside, to take away, remove; used of removing idols, high places, and reproach.
Hebrew rachaq (H7368) — to be or become far, to remove far away; the verb measuring the distance in Psalm 103:12.
Hebrew gebuwl (H1366) — border, boundary, landmark; the ancient stone of Proverbs 22:28.
Greek metabaino (G3327) — to pass from one place to another, to remove; used of the mountain removing at faith's word.
Greek kineo (G2795) — to move, to remove; the verb of removing the candlestick out of its place.
usage: “So far hath he removed our transgressions from us” — the distance is chosen because it cannot be measured.
“Remove not the ancient landmark” — boundaries received from the fathers are not the sons' to shift.
“I will remove thy candlestick” — a church's light is held on the condition of repentance.

pos: v. (to place a body in the earth or a tomb; rendering Hebrew qabar, Greek thapto)
etymology: From Saxon byrgan, to hide or cover. The patriarchs bought fields to bury in, and the Apostle makes burial the very figure of baptism — so the word joins the hope of resurrection to a plot of ground.
biblical_def: To bury is to lay a body in the earth, and Scripture treats the act as a duty of love and a confession of hope. Abraham's first purchase in the promised land was a grave: “I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight” (Genesis 23:4). A man who owned nothing else in Canaan owned a tomb, and it was an act of faith in the promise rather than a concession to death. The gospel itself is preached with a burial in the middle of it: Christ “was buried, and… he rose again the third day according to the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4). The burial is not a detail between the cross and the empty tomb; it is the proof that He was truly dead, and it stands in the creed for that reason. From there the Apostle draws the believer's baptism: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Burial is the picture immersion makes. Our Lord also subordinates the duty to Himself when the two collide: “Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).
webster_summary: To deposit a deceased body in the grave; to inter; to cover with earth; to hide or conceal. Scripture makes burial both an office of love toward the dead and the figure by which baptism preaches death and resurrection with Christ.
webster_full: BURY, v.t. [Sax. byrgan, to hide, to bury.] To deposit a deceased person in the grave; to inter a corpse; to entomb.
2. To cover with earth, as seed sown.
3. To hide; to conceal; to overwhelm; to cover with anything.
4. To withdraw or conceal in retirement; as, to bury one's self in a cloister.
5. To commit to oblivion; to forget; as, to bury an injury.
BURIAL, n. The act of burying a deceased person; interment; sepulture.
scriptures: Genesis 23:4
I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.
1 Corinthians 15:4
And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:
Romans 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Matthew 8:22
But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead.
corruption_summary: The funeral has been remade into a celebration that refuses to name death, and with the naming goes the resurrection hope that made Christian burial a confession rather than a disposal.
corruption_paragraphs: Christian burial was always a sermon. The body was treated with honour because it is the Lord's and will be raised; the grave was a bed rather than an end; and the words spoken over it named death plainly enough for the promise to answer it. Much modern practice has reversed both halves. The service is recast as a celebration of a life, death is not named, and the body — the thing Scripture says is sown in corruption and raised in incorruption — is often hurried out of sight beforehand so that nothing interrupts the tone. What is lost is not solemnity for its own sake but the occasion for hope, since a hope that answers nothing comforts no one.

Behind the practice lies a doctrinal drift: resurrection reduced to the survival of a soul or to a memory kept alive among the living. Scripture's burial language will not reduce. Abraham bought a field to bury in because he expected to receive the land; Christ was buried because He was genuinely dead; the believer is buried with Christ in baptism precisely so that he may walk in newness of life now and be raised bodily hereafter. Recover the plain confession, and the grave becomes what the fathers called it, a place of sleeping.
roots_summary: Hebrew qabar (to bury) and qeber (grave, sepulchre) govern the patriarchal narratives; Greek thapto (to bury) and suntapto (to bury together with) give Romans 6:4 its force.
roots_lines: Hebrew qabar (H6912) — to bury; the verb of Genesis 23 and of the repeated notices that a man was buried with his fathers.
Hebrew qeber (H6913) — grave, sepulchre, burying place; the noun Abraham sought a possession of.
Greek thapto (G2290) — to bury; used in the gospel summary of 1 Corinthians 15:4.
Greek sunthapto (G4916) — to bury together with; the compound behind “buried with him by baptism” in Romans 6:4.
Greek mnemeion (G3419) — a tomb, sepulchre; the borrowed tomb from which our Lord rose.
usage: “That I may bury my dead out of my sight” — the first possession in the land of promise was a grave.
“He was buried, and… he rose again the third day” — burial stands in the gospel summary as proof of real death.
“Buried with him by baptism into death” — the ordinance pictures the burial it proclaims.

pos: v. (to force or urge along; to expel; rendering Hebrew garash, nadaph, Greek ekballo)
etymology: From Saxon drifan, to urge or impel. The word's first appearance in Scripture is the expulsion from Eden, and it keeps that weight: what is driven is not led but forced, whether chaff by wind or a man from a garden.
biblical_def: To drive is to move a thing by force rather than by consent. Its first use sets the pattern: “So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). The driving out is judicial, and the guarded way says that man cannot simply walk back. From that beginning the word carries the sense of what has no root and no weight of its own: “The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Psalm 1:4). The righteous man of the Psalm is a planted tree; the ungodly is chaff, and the judgment needs no violence beyond a wind, because there is nothing there to hold. The New Testament applies the same figure to the double-minded man in prayer: he “is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (James 1:6), which is why such a man is told not to expect to receive anything of the Lord. Scripture also puts the verb to a merciful use in the discipline of children: “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him” (Proverbs 22:15). Folly is bound in and must be driven out.
webster_summary: To urge or press forward by force; to impel; to compel to move; to expel or chase away. Scripture uses it of the expulsion from Eden, of chaff before the wind, of the unstable soul, and of folly driven from a child by correction.
webster_full: DRIVE, v.t. [Sax. drifan, to urge, impel.] To impel or urge forward by force; to force; to move by physical force; as, to drive cattle; to drive a nail.
2. To compel or urge by other means than absolute physical force; to constrain; as, hunger drives men to labor.
3. To chase; to hunt; to expel; as, to drive an enemy from his ground.
4. To guide and regulate the course of a carriage or the beasts that draw it.
5. To carry on; to prosecute; as, to drive a trade.
DRIVE, v.i. To be forced along; to be impelled; as, a ship drives before the wind. To rush with violence; to aim at or tend to.
scriptures: Genesis 3:24
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.
Psalm 1:4
The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.
James 1:6
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
Proverbs 22:15
Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.
corruption_summary: The expulsion from Eden is read as a myth about growing up rather than as a judicial act, and the correction that drives folly from a child is renamed as harm — so both of Scripture's drivings are explained away.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 3:24 is regularly retold as the story of humanity leaving innocence behind, a necessary passage into maturity, with the cherubim and the flaming sword treated as symbols of an inward loss. That reading empties the sentence. The man is driven, by God, from a real garden, and the way to the tree of life is guarded so that he cannot return on his own terms — which is the whole reason a way back had to be opened by Another. Where the expulsion becomes a metaphor for maturation, the atonement becomes unnecessary, since nothing objective was ever barred.

The second corruption touches Proverbs 22:15. Correction administered by a father under God is now widely classed as harm as such, without distinction between the rod of correction and the cruelty Scripture equally condemns. The proverb states a diagnosis before it prescribes: foolishness is bound in the heart of a child, and something bound must be driven out rather than waited out. Fathers are to be gentle, never provoking their children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4), and they are to correct. Recover both halves and the word keeps its proper severity in judgment and its proper tenderness in the home. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the modern re-description of correction as 'harm' in order to rebut it
roots_summary: Hebrew garash (to drive out, expel) is the verb of Eden and of the nations driven before Israel; nadaph (to drive asunder) gives Psalm 1 its chaff; Greek ekballo (to cast out) and elauno (to drive) carry the New Testament senses.
roots_lines: Hebrew garash (H1644) — to drive out, cast out, expel; used of Adam from the garden and of the Canaanites from the land.
Hebrew nadaph (H5086) — to drive asunder, to scatter as chaff before wind; the verb of Psalm 1:4.
Hebrew muwcar (H4148) — chastening, correction, discipline; the instrument that drives folly out in Proverbs 22:15.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, drive out; used of casting out devils and of the Spirit driving our Lord into the wilderness.
Greek anemizo (G416) — to be driven by the wind; the picture of the wavering man in James 1:6.
usage: “So he drove out the man” — the expulsion is judicial, and the way back is guarded.
“Like the chaff which the wind driveth away” — what has no root needs no violence to remove it.
“The rod of correction shall drive it far from him” — bound folly is driven out, not outgrown.

pos: v. (to lift up, erect, or restore to life; rendering Hebrew quwm, Greek egeiro)
etymology: From the Gothic and Saxon root meaning to rear or set upright. Scripture reserves its highest use for God: He raises up judges, kings, and prophets, and He raised up Christ from the dead.
biblical_def: To raise is to lift what is down, and in Scripture the decisive raising is God's raising of the dead. The Father's act is stated as the ground of the church's preaching: “Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it” (Acts 2:24). Peter's reason is worth weighing — not merely that death did not hold Him, but that it was not possible that it should. The Son also claims the act as His own work and attaches it to every believer: “this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day” (John 6:40). The resurrection of Christ is never left as a solitary wonder; it is the first of a harvest. Paul ties the believer's justification to it — Christ “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification” (Romans 4:25) — so that the empty tomb is the Father's public acceptance of the payment made at the cross. And the same power is promised to us: “he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you” (2 Corinthians 4:14). The verb therefore holds the gospel together at both ends.
webster_summary: To lift upward; to set upright; to erect; to rouse or stir up; to restore to life. Scripture's chief use is God raising Christ from the dead and, by the same power, raising up His people at the last day.
webster_full: RAISE, v.t. To lift; to take up; to heave; to lift from a low or reclining position; as, to raise a stone or weight.
2. To set upright; to erect; to build; as, to raise a wall or a house.
3. To rouse; to stir up; to excite; as, to raise a tumult; to raise the passions.
4. To bring to life from the dead; to restore from death; as, to raise the dead.
5. To cause to grow; to procure to be produced or bred; as, to raise corn or cattle.
6. To collect; to levy; to get together; as, to raise money or an army.
scriptures: Acts 2:24
Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.
John 6:40
And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Romans 4:25
Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.
2 Corinthians 4:14
Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you.
corruption_summary: Resurrection has been spiritualized into renewal — rising above circumstances, new beginnings, the survival of influence — where Scripture means a body raised, a tomb emptied, and a justification publicly declared.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common corruption keeps the vocabulary of rising and abandons the fact. Easter is preached as the perennial triumph of hope over despair, of spring over winter, of the human spirit over its circumstances. Every one of those is a metaphor borrowed from an event that is then quietly denied. Peter's sermon in Acts 2 is not a meditation on renewal; it is testimony that a particular man was raised up because death could not hold Him, offered to hearers who could walk to the tomb. Where the event goes, the justification of Romans 4:25 goes with it, and the church is left preaching a mood.

A subtler drift concedes the resurrection of Christ and evaporates ours, treating the believer's hope as the soul's survival rather than the body's raising. Scripture will not divide them: the same power that raised the Lord Jesus raises us also (2 Corinthians 4:14), and the promise of John 6:40 is fixed to the last day rather than to the hour of death. The Christian hope is not that a man escapes his body but that he receives it again glorified. Recover that, and the word regains the weight the creeds gave it.
roots_summary: Hebrew quwm (to arise, stand up) and 'uwr (to rouse, stir up) supply the Old Testament sense of raising up deliverers; Greek egeiro (to waken, raise up) and anistemi (to cause to stand again) are the resurrection verbs.
roots_lines: Hebrew quwm (H6965) — to arise, stand, be established; used of God raising up judges, prophets, and a Prophet like unto Moses.
Hebrew 'uwr (H5782) — to rouse, awake, stir up; used of stirring up a spirit or a people to action.
Greek egeiro (G1453) — to waken, to raise up; the standard New Testament verb for God raising Christ from the dead.
Greek anistemi (G450) — to cause to stand up, to rise again; the verb behind anastasis, resurrection.
Greek anastasis (G386) — a standing up again, resurrection; the noun naming the hope in its settled form.
usage: “It was not possible that he should be holden of it” — the resurrection was necessary, not merely actual.
“I will raise him up at the last day” — the believer's raising is promised by the Son Himself.
“Raised again for our justification” — the empty tomb is the Father's receipt for the cross.

pos: v. (to put or place down; to set in position; rendering Hebrew yacad, suwm, Greek tithemi)
etymology: From Saxon lecgan, to place. Scripture's two great uses are architectural and sacrificial: God lays a foundation stone in Zion, and the Good Shepherd lays down His life.
biblical_def: To lay is to set a thing deliberately in its place, and Scripture's first great use is architectural. The LORD announces what He Himself will put down: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste” (Isaiah 28:16). Each word is load-bearing — tried, because the stone has been proved; precious, because of its worth; sure, because what rests on it will stand — and the response required is belief rather than haste. The Apostle identifies the stone and forbids competitors: “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Men may build well or badly on it, but no man may lay another. The second great use is sacrificial, and our Lord makes it the mark of the true shepherd against the hireling: “Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again” (John 10:17). The laying down is voluntary, and it is paired with a taking again, so that the cross is never separated from the resurrection. The same verb measures His poverty in the days of His flesh: “the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20).
webster_summary: To place in a lying position; to set or put down; to deposit; to impose or charge. Scripture's weightiest uses are the foundation stone God lays in Zion and the life the Good Shepherd lays down of Himself.
webster_full: LAY, v.t. [Sax. lecgan, to place.] To place in a lying position; to set or place in a horizontal direction; as, to lay a book on the table.
2. To put or place in general; to deposit; as, to lay a foundation.
3. To impose, as a burden, tax, duty or command; as, to lay a tax on land.
4. To spread on a surface; as, to lay colors on canvas.
5. To bring forth and deposit, as eggs.
6. To wager; to stake; as, to lay a sum of money on the event.
LAY, v.i. To bring forth eggs. To wager or bet. [Note: to lay is transitive; to lie is intransitive.]
scriptures: Isaiah 28:16
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
1 Corinthians 3:11
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
John 10:17
Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.
Matthew 8:20
And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
corruption_summary: Foundations are treated as interchangeable — a church may be built on vision, personality, or cause — where Scripture says the only foundation is already laid and no man may lay another.
corruption_paragraphs: The practical error of the age is not usually a denial that Christ is the foundation but a quiet addition of others beside Him. A congregation is founded on a man's gifts, a movement on a grievance, a ministry on a method, and Christ is confessed at the level of doctrine while something else bears the actual weight. 1 Corinthians 3:11 addresses exactly that situation: Paul is writing to a church dividing over teachers, and he does not say that Christ is the best foundation among several but that no other can be laid. The test is simple — remove the man, the cause, or the method, and see whether the building stands.

A second corruption touches John 10:17. The laying down of Christ's life is often described as a tragedy He suffered rather than an act He performed, and the words that follow in the passage are dropped: no man taketh it from Him; He lays it down of Himself, and He has power to take it again. That voluntary character is what makes the cross an offering rather than a martyrdom, and it is the ground of the Father's stated love. Recover it, and the shepherd's laying down of His life stands over against every hireling who flees.
roots_summary: Hebrew yacad (to found, lay a foundation) governs Isaiah 28:16; suwm (to put, place, set) is the common verb of placing; Greek tithemi (to put, place, lay down) covers both foundation-laying and the laying down of life.
roots_lines: Hebrew yacad (H3245) — to found, to lay a foundation; the verb of the tried stone laid in Zion.
Hebrew suwm (H7760) — to put, place, set, appoint; the ordinary verb of laying a thing in its place.
Hebrew pinnah (H6438) — corner; the source of the corner stone figure that Isaiah and the Apostles apply to Christ.
Greek tithemi (G5087) — to place, to lay down; used of laying a foundation and of Christ laying down His life.
Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation; the noun of 1 Corinthians 3:11, which no man may re-lay.
usage: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone” — the foundation is God's own placing, not the builders'.
“Other foundation can no man lay” — the exclusion is of possibility, not merely of preference.
“I lay down my life, that I might take it again” — the offering is voluntary and paired with the resurrection.
